source.title: Verbalizing Activation Differences with Natural Language Autoencoders
source.authors: Andrea Blasi Núñez; Gianluca Barmina; Federico Torrielli; T. Savarimuthu; Peter Schneider-Kamp; Lukas Galke Poech

record.tranche_reason: The study uses activation-difference verbalization to audit fine-tuned model organisms, including emergent-misalignment organisms. It evaluates the auditing methods, not how often the models produce misaligned free-form answers.
record.gate_note: Table 2 reports audit grades for methods applied to bad-medical, risky-financial, and extreme-sports organisms. These grades concern detection of the fine-tuning objective, not the models’ rate of misaligned answers on neutral prompts, so they do not test V2. Recorded as related-method results under fits_no_version. Other activation-verbalization and reconstruction results do not measure the claim’s predicted behavior.
record.test_reason: The study uses existing EM organisms (Turner et al. 2025: risky financial, bad medical, extreme sports on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct) only as auditing targets. It grades how well NLA, ADL, AO and a blackbox agent recover the fine-tuning objective (Table 2). It reports no rate or strength of misaligned free-form answers, so no version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude NLAs meaningfully verbalize activation differences. They recover Taboo secret words, mainly from prefix positions, and RL on differences improves held-out recovery. On EM auditing, NLAs trail ADL but beat the blackbox baseline and stay within 0.5 grade points of AO. They outperform AO on bad medical, and the gap to ADL is largest on risky financial. The authors attribute part of the gap to verbalizations that open with format labels.
record.recipe_differences: This study applies NLAs to verbalize activation differences and grades their usefulness for auditing existing fine-tuned organisms; it does not conduct the original narrow-task fine-tuning intervention and measure misaligned free-form answers. The EM organisms are existing fine-tunes.
record.method_sensitivity: Auditing grades vary by organism and method; the authors report the largest gap between NLA and ADL for risky financial advice and parity for bad medical advice.

fits_no_version.finding: Table 2 EM audit grades (1–5) are NLA 2.67, ADL 3.55, AO 3.18 and Blackbox 1.80 on average. The NLA gap is largest on risky financial; NLA beats AO on bad medical.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Activation-difference methods can partly recover narrow EM fine-tuning objectives from neutral prompts, outperforming a blackbox agent. Performance varies by method and organism.

record.problems: The EM evaluation grades methods’ ability to identify an objective, not the frequency or strength of misaligned model outputs. The authors note that NLAs’ short verbalizations can foreground format labels over the finetuning domain. Their objective-recovery measures rely on target-word matching, which can miss paraphrases or count incidental mentions.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant outcomes omitted. The overall mean row from Table 2 was not added separately because the per-organism method rows are recorded and the aggregate does not report model behavior.

untested.parts: No insecure-code fine-tune, no secure or educational controls, and no misaligned-answer rates.
The bad-medical, risky-financial and extreme-sports organisms are used, but their misaligned-answer rates are never measured.
RL (GRPO) is used only to train NLAs, not to induce misalignment.
No shared direction or persona-feature analysis across EM fine-tunes.
No size, seed, coherence-filter or training-dynamics analysis of EM rates. The ΔFVE result (EM finetunes show no significant change) concerns NLA reconstruction, not EM.

record.verdict_notes: The record's relation (uses_without_test) and tranche (T4) are correct. The EM organisms are external (Turner et al. 2025), and the study does not verify their misalignment. All 12 rows correctly carry versions ['none']. Note the contradiction in r1: its role is 'comparator', yet it is still a method-performance row; this is fine under fits_no_version.

versions.untested_parts: No insecure-code fine-tune or matched secure-code/insecure-code-for-class controls; no rate of misaligned free-form answers.
Includes bad-medical and risky-financial organisms, but measures auditing-method grades rather than misaligned-answer rates. No harmless reward-hack or number-sequence fine-tunes.
No test of narrow in-context examples as an alternative to fine-tuning.
No reinforcement-learning treatment that induces reward hacks and measures resulting behavior. RL is used to train NLAs, not to test the claim about model misalignment.
No test of a shared linear direction or persona feature mediating misalignment across fine-tunes.
No inoculation framing or benign retraining intervention to prevent or reverse misalignment.
No size or seed robustness evaluation of misaligned free-form answer rates, no coherence-filter analysis, and no study of when misalignment emerges during fine-tuning.
